blocks.text: **The task.** Given a list of non-overlapping intervals **already sorted by start**, insert a new interval and merge where necessary.
Why this is not just merge again
You could append and re-run merge, but that throws away the sortedness you were given and costs O(N log N). Since the input is already ordered, **O(N)** is achievable.
Walk once, and the intervals fall into three groups:

items: **Entirely before** the new interval — copy them across untouched.
**Overlapping** it — absorb them, widening the new interval.

blocks.text: Phase one uses `intervals[i][1] < start` — this interval **ends** before the new one starts, so there is no contact at all.

Phase two uses `intervals[i][0] <= end` — this interval **starts** at or before the new one ends, so they touch. Both `start` and `end` are widened, because an absorbed interval may extend the range in either direction.
**Time: O(N)** — `i` only moves forward, so all three loops together are one pass.
This linear solution is the entire point of the problem. Producing the O(N log N) re-sort version answers it, but misses what it was asking.
